t: Formal Verification Tools: What Formal Verification Is: Proof Instead of Testing
title: Formal Verification Tools: What Formal Verification Is: Proof Instead of Testing
description: Testing shows the presence of bugs; verification proves their absence — for the properties proven. The seL4 microkernel is the landmark: a complete, machine-checked proof that its C implementation refines its specification — no buffer overflows, no null dereferences, ever, in the verified configuration. Model checkers (CBMC, SPIN) exhaustively explore state spaces; proof assistants (Coq, Isabelle) host human-guided proofs. It is expensive, and for the most critical software, it is worth it.
key_facts: Proof of absence for proven properties

t: Formal Verification Tools: seL4: The Verified Microkernel
title: Formal Verification Tools: seL4: The Verified Microkernel
description: seL4 is a small, fast microkernel with an unprecedented assurance story: functional correctness proven in Isabelle/HOL, plus proofs of integrity, confidentiality, and (for some configs) real-time behavior. Around 10,000 lines of C, each covered by the proof. It runs in defense, automotive, and medical systems where failure is unacceptable. Using seL4 means building on a foundation that cannot have the bug classes testing usually hunts.

t: Formal Verification Tools: Refinement: From Spec to Code
title: Formal Verification Tools: Refinement: From Spec to Code
description: The seL4 proof technique is refinement: an abstract specification, an executable specification, and the C code — with machine-checked proofs that each refines the one above. Bugs cannot hide between the spec and the code because the proof bridges them. This is the gold standard's shape: not 'the code is correct' but 'the code correctly implements this specification' — with the specification itself reviewed for capturing the intent.

t: Formal Verification Tools: Model Checking: Exhaustive Exploration
title: Formal Verification Tools: Model Checking: Exhaustive Exploration
description: Model checkers like CBMC (bounded model checking for C) and SPIN (protocol verification) explore all behaviors up to a bound: every interleaving, every input in range. CBMC proves the absence of buffer overflows and assertion violations in C functions — push-button verification for the properties it covers. The bound is the fine print: 'correct for all inputs up to N loop iterations' is strong but bounded, and the bound is stated.
key_facts: Explore all behaviors to a bound
CBMC for C, SPIN for protocols

t: Formal Verification Tools: Your First Proof: An Invariant
title: Formal Verification Tools: Your First Proof: An Invariant
description: The hello-world of verification: prove a loop invariant — e.g., a counter that never exceeds its bound. Write the invariant, let the checker verify it holds initially and is preserved by each iteration. It is small, but it is the whole method in miniature: state the property, prove it inductively. From here the properties grow: memory safety, then functional correctness, then security properties.

t: Formal Verification Tools: Proof Assistants: Coq and Isabelle
title: Formal Verification Tools: Proof Assistants: Coq and Isabelle
description: Proof assistants (Coq, Isabelle/HOL) are where deep proofs are built: the human guides, the machine checks every step. seL4's proof is Isabelle; CompCert's (verified C compiler) is Coq. Learning one is learning to think with total precision — the assistant accepts no hand-waving. The investment is large; the payoff is certainty about the things that must be certain.

t: Formal Verification Tools: Applying Verification to Protocols
title: Formal Verification Tools: Applying Verification to Protocols
description: Verification shines on protocols: model the handshake in SPIN or TLA+, specify 'the key is never exposed' or 'both parties agree', and let the checker find the interleaving that breaks it — or prove none exists. Protocol bugs are logic bugs, and logic bugs are what checkers eat for breakfast. Every security protocol worth deploying deserves the model-checker's attention before it ships.

t: Formal Verification Tools: Verified Toolchains: CompCert and Beyond
title: Formal Verification Tools: Verified Toolchains: CompCert and Beyond
description: The compiler is part of the trusted base — so verify it: CompCert is a C compiler with a machine-checked proof that the generated assembly preserves the source semantics. Verified toolchains (CompCert, CakeML) close the loop: verified source, verified compilation, verified binary. The practical use is the critical component compiled with CompCert — the proof chain unbroken from spec to silicon.

t: Formal Verification Tools: Defensive Uses: The Unbreakable Core
title: Formal Verification Tools: Defensive Uses: The Unbreakable Core
description: Formal verification's defensive value is the trustworthy core: a verified kernel, verified crypto implementations (HACL*, Fiat), verified parsers for critical protocols. Around the verified core, traditional engineering; inside it, proof. The architecture is defense in depth with the innermost layer proven. For the systems that must not fail — flight control, crypto, access control — verification is the appropriate standard of care.

t: Formal Verification Tools: The Cost: When Verification Pays
title: Formal Verification Tools: The Cost: When Verification Pays
description: Verification is expensive — person-years for seL4-scale proofs — so the decision is economic: verify the small, critical, stable core (kernels, crypto, protocols), test the large and changing. The cost curve favors reuse: a verified component amortizes across every system that uses it. The question is never 'verify everything' but 'what is the cheapest component whose failure is the most expensive'.

t: Formal Verification Tools: Debugging: The Failed Proof
title: Formal Verification Tools: Debugging: The Failed Proof
description: A failed proof is a successful analysis: the prover's counterexample is a bug report — the exact scenario violating the property. Debugging is reading the counterexample, understanding whether the code or the property is wrong (often the property was too strong), and fixing accordingly. Failed proofs teach: every one is either a bug found or a specification improved.
key_facts: Code wrong or property too strong

t: Formal Verification Tools: Composition: Verified Components, Safe Systems
title: Formal Verification Tools: Composition: Verified Components, Safe Systems
description: The frontier is composition: proving that verified components compose into verified systems — the kernel's proof plus the application's proof equals the system's guarantee. This is hard (assumptions must align) and it is where the field is going. The practical step today is assume-guarantee reasoning: each component proven against its contract, integration checked against the contracts.

t: Formal Verification Tools: Testing: Proof and Test Together
title: Formal Verification Tools: Testing: Proof and Test Together
description: Proof and testing are complements: prove the critical properties, test the rest — and test the proof's assumptions (the hardware behaves as modeled, the compiler is correct). seL4's proof assumes the hardware and the C semantics; testing validates the assumptions. The mature practice is the belt and suspenders: proof where it counts, testing everywhere, and explicit about which is which.

title: Formal Verification Tools: Real-World Pattern: Verified Update Channel
description: A complete pattern: a device's update mechanism — parser, signature check, installer — built on seL4 with the parser and crypto verified, the update protocol model-checked. The device accepts only proven-correct updates through a proven-correct channel. The attack surface that matters most is the one with the strongest guarantee.
